reception.text: The Associated Press carried the order's full text, and papers printed it the next morning.
reception.source: Riverside Enterprise and Stockton Daily Independent, October 6, 1904; Chicago Daily Tribune, October 6, 1904

reception.text: The Democratic Los Angeles Herald's editorial column said of Payne only that close application to his duties seemed to have overtaxed his strength, and kept the post-office fraud charges in a separate paragraph.

political_impact.text: The Washington departments closed from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. on the day of the funeral, Friday, October 7, and flags flew at half-mast on public buildings until the funeral.
political_impact.source: EO 271, in Wight, Henry Clay Payne: A Life (1907), p. 169

political_impact.text: Robert J. Wynne, First Assistant Postmaster-General, was named acting Postmaster-General the day after Payne's death and Postmaster-General on October 10, serving until March 1905.
Five weeks before the election, the Democratic vice-presidential candidate, Henry G. Davis, was attacking the post-office frauds and the Republicans' refusal of a congressional investigation.

reception.text: The San Francisco Call reported that civil-service rules would reach the canal commission's employees, apart from presidential appointees, laborers and "about thirty places."

political_impact.text: By December the Civil Service Commission was circulating recruiting notices for the Isthmus through its local boards.

legacy.text: The order was an early piece of the personnel system that would build the Panama Canal.

related.note: Signed the same day, excepting twenty-three classes of canal position from examination.

political_impact.text: The Civil Service Commission explained that the waiver was made at the Isthmian Canal Commission's request, because the service's needs could not be met without hiring non-citizens.
political_impact.source: U.S. Civil Service Commission, Twenty-second Annual Report (1905), p. 69

later_actions.text: President Truman's Executive Order 9830 revoked the citizenship waiver.
President Truman's Executive Order 9830 revoked the rule against hiring outside the civil-service rules for classified-type work.

political_impact.text: As amended by July 12, 1905, the Washington labor rules rated applicants on "physical fitness and efficiency" rather than "skill and efficiency" and raised the passing rating from 70 to 85.
political_impact.source: U.S. Civil Service Commission, Twenty-second Annual Report (1905), pp. 95–99

legacy.text: The labor regulations fed into the slow, decades-long extension of the merit system to the whole federal workforce.

legacy.text: The forest guards it classified passed with the reserves to the Department of Agriculture in 1905, where the reserves became the foundation of the Forest Service.

political_impact.text: Giving the Dead Letter Office post to James Rankin Young, just out of Congress after three terms, is the group's clearest example of the standing complaint that appointments without examination wore down the merit system.

legacy.text: Young held the Dead Letter Office post until 1913.
